s-1-0.title: The short answer
s-1-0.previewHtml: (Structural inference from the capability-loss matrix of Decision guide and the cutoff lab's census (Appendix A, §A.3) and reference stack (Appendix A, §A.4)) A server in Taiwan is the price of entry, not the answer. Hosted abroad, a service cannot load, message, serve its data or sign anyone in at Global Cutoff, and no measure in Chapter 4 changes that. Hosted on the island, it still fails to load as shipped, because its names, certificates, clocks and embedded files answer from abroad. An ordinary software engineer can keep what users touch working, loading pages, signing in, messaging and paying at the counter, on networks that meet on the island, but only with work done before the cables fail, and the lab confirmed it only for the first hours. No engineer on the island can keep push notifications, online checkout through foreign gateways, software updates or control of cloud infrastructure.

s-1-1.title: Why connectivity is a crisis problem
s-1-1.previewHtml: Daily life and its records now depend on continuous connectivity, so a network failure affects more of daily life than it once did. A study of provider failures on a university network observes that the more users depend on connectivity, the greater the impact of losing it (Duarte et al., IFIP Networking, 2015). Households show the same change: cheap unlimited mobile data has moved family files, notes, and passwords into cloud services (Cyborg Resilience Co-Lab, 家庭用數位防災包, August 2026).

s-1-2.title: Cables, landing stations, and power
s-1-2.previewHtml: Taiwan's link to the global internet depends on three physical layers: the submarine cables, the landing stations where the cables come ashore, and electricity. Electricity runs the cables, the landing stations, and the domestic network behind them. This section describes each layer and how the three layers fail together. Submarine cables, landing stations, and international transit capacity and Microwave and satellite fallback paths, capacity and civilian availability analyze the cables, the landing stations, and the fallback paths as shared dependencies.

s-1-3.title: Threat contexts
s-1-3.previewHtml: Four threat contexts frame this report: peacetime and the gray zone, a blockade, a landing by the People's Liberation Army (PLA), and a mega-quake. A threat context is a geopolitical or natural condition, and the report does not treat it as the cause of a disruption level of Chapter 2. Any threat context might produce any disruption level, or none. The report therefore does not organize its analysis by threat context.

s-1-4.title: What this report is
s-1-4.previewHtml: This report analyzes the shared dependencies beneath Taiwan's internet services, not the services themselves. A shared dependency is a component that many otherwise independent services rely on, such as the Domain Name System (DNS), certificate trust, push delivery, or a cloud control plane. When a shared dependency fails, the services that rely on it fail together. A failing product appears in the report only as a symptom, which the report uses as evidence for the dependency beneath the product.

s-1-5.title: How to read this report
s-1-5.previewHtml: A reader with time for one page reads The short answer, which answers the report's two questions from the evidence and lists what is still unknown. The chapters then move from effect to dependency to remedy. Chapter 2 defines three disruption levels by their effect: 50% Degradation, Global Cutoff, and Island Partition. The three levels form an escalation ladder, in which each level includes every effect of the level below it (The disruption ladder). Chapter 3 traces each level through the 26 shared dependencies that carry its effects to civilian services, starting from four fault trees with 13 top events (Orientation), and closes with the human-organizational preconditions, four of which are leaves in the trees (Human-organizational dependencies). A fault tree is a diagram of the faults that can cause one failure.

s-2-0.title: The disruption ladder
s-2-0.previewHtml: This chapter defines three disruption levels: 50% Degradation (降載), Global Cutoff, and Island Partition. The three levels form an escalation ladder: each level includes every effect of the level below it.

s-2-1.title: 50% Degradation
s-2-1.previewHtml: 50% Degradation is the first level of the escalation ladder. The whole island loses approximately 50% of its bandwidth to the global internet, and the domestic network stays intact. The domestic network means users, internet service providers (ISPs), the domestic internet exchange points (IXPs: TPIX, TWIX, STUIX), and services hosted in Taiwan. The report calls the network's behavior at this level brownout (slow, lossy service), and keeps the name 50% Degradation for the level itself.

s-2-2.title: Global Cutoff
s-2-2.previewHtml: In Global Cutoff, the island loses 100% of its bandwidth to the global internet, while the domestic network keeps working normally. The domestic network has three parts: the links between internet service providers (ISPs) on the island, the domestic internet exchange points (IXPs: TPIX, TWIX and STUIX), and locally hosted services. Global Cutoff completes the loss that 50% Degradation causes at half scale: bandwidth to the global internet falls to zero on every international cable.

s-2-3.title: Island Partition
s-2-3.previewHtml: Island Partition is the worst case on the escalation ladder, because two failures happen together. The north–south domestic long-haul trunks (the main long-distance links inside Taiwan) are cut, so northern Taiwan cannot reach southern Taiwan. At the same time, all global connectivity is lost.

s-2-4.title: Interfaces
s-2-4.previewHtml: Chapter 3 links to this chapter through the simulated scenarios. At each disruption level, every trace of a shared dependency in Chapter 3 covers each simulated scenario that 50% Degradation through Island Partition list under that level. Each trace presents the simulated scenarios as a nested list, in the form set out in How to read a SPOF walk.

s-3-0.title: Orientation
s-3-0.previewHtml: Chapter 2 defined three disruption levels by their effect. This chapter traces each level through the shared dependencies that carry it to civilian services. A shared dependency is a deep dependency that many otherwise-independent services sit on.

s-3-1.title: Physical
s-3-1.previewHtml: The physical layer group holds the cables, landing stations, radio paths, timing signals, and facilities on which every other layer group runs. Its most concentrated element is the international cable plant, analyzed in Submarine cables, landing stations, and international transit capacity. The plant has 15 international cables, which land at four coastal stations and carry 95–99% of the island's international traffic (Taiwan Center for Security Studies; MODA press release, April 2026).

s-3-1-1.title: Submarine cables, landing stations, and international transit capacity
s-3-1-1.previewHtml: Shared dependency: When the cables and their landing stations fail, Offshore path holds fails unless the microwave and satellite fallback paths of Microwave and satellite fallback paths, capacity and civilian availability carry the international capacity in their place. With Offshore path holds fall Your users get notified, Your cloud-hosted data is readable and writable, Online checkout approves, You can ship and update software, You can control your infrastructure, and You can stand up new address space; Your users load your service, Your users message and call each other, Your users log in, You can see your service and be paged and You can detect and respond to an attack survive only while Domestic path holds carries them.

Where both are gone, Your users get notified, Your cloud-hosted data is readable and writable, Online checkout approves, You can ship and update software, You can control your infrastructure, and You can stand up new address space fall with Offshore path holds, while Your users load your service, Your users message and call each other, Your users log in, You can see your service and be paged and You can detect and respond to an attack survive only while Domestic path holds carries them.

s-3-1-3.previewHtml: Shared dependency: When the shared timing source fails, Time holds fails with it (GNSS is an AND child there, so nothing in the “What your service sits on: four fault trees” section's trees routes around it), and with Time holds fall Your users load your service, Your users log in, and Online checkout approves. The authenticator-app alternative under Second-factor delivery rests on Time holds alone, so it falls too, leaving second-factor delivery to the messaging infrastructure of Messaging infrastructure.

Your users load your service, Your users message and call each other, Your users log in, You can see your service and be paged and You can detect and respond to an attack survive only while Offshore path holds carries them, and You can reach your own machines only while the mesh VPN overlay of Mesh VPN overlay coordination (lighthouse nodes; Yggdrasil, tinc) holds its Path gate.

Domestic path holds fails with it, taking Your domestically hosted data is readable and writable and Card-present domestic authorization clears; Your users load your service, Your users message and call each other, Your users log in, You can see your service and be paged and You can detect and respond to an attack survive only while Offshore path holds carries them.

s-3-1-6.previewHtml: Shared dependency: When site power runs out, Domestic path holds fails with it, taking Your domestically hosted data is readable and writable and Card-present domestic authorization clears; Your users load your service, Your users message and call each other, Your users log in, You can see your service and be paged and You can detect and respond to an attack survive only while Offshore path holds carries them, and You can reach your own machines survives only while the mesh VPN overlay carries it.

s-3-2.title: Network
s-3-2.previewHtml: The network layer group differs from the physical layer group in one respect. Its chokepoints can waste or cut international capacity while the cables themselves stay physically intact. Four shared dependencies of routing and coordination have this property.

s-3-2-1.title: Concentrated international gateway, administrative kill-switch and adversary-forced rerouting
s-3-2-1.previewHtml: Shared dependency: When the gateway nodes fail, Offshore path holds fails with them (the gateway is an AND child of Offshore path holds, so neither cable nor satellite capacity routes around it), and with Offshore path holds fall Your users get notified, Your cloud-hosted data is readable and writable, Online checkout approves, You can ship and update software, You can control your infrastructure, and You can stand up new address space. Five top events survive only while Domestic path holds carries them: Your users load your service, Your users message and call each other, Your users log in, You can see your service and be paged and You can detect and respond to an attack.

s-3-2-2.title: Mesh VPN overlay coordination (lighthouse nodes; Yggdrasil, tinc)
s-3-2-2.previewHtml: Shared dependency: When overlay coordination fails, You can reach your own machines survives only while Domestic path holds, the other alternative under its Path gate. No other top event in the fault trees of What your service sits on: four fault trees depends on overlay coordination.

s-3-2-3.title: Weak domestic peering and TW-to-TW tromboning
s-3-2-3.previewHtml: Shared dependency: When domestic peering fails, or when domestic traffic is forced offshore and back, Domestic path holds fails with it, and with Domestic path holds fall Your domestically hosted data is readable and writable and Card-present domestic authorization clears. Five top events survive only while Offshore path holds, namely Your users load your service, Your users message and call each other, Your users log in, You can see your service and be paged and You can detect and respond to an attack, and You can reach your own machines survives only while the mesh VPN overlay of Mesh VPN overlay coordination (lighthouse nodes; Yggdrasil, tinc) holds its Path gate.

s-3-2-4.title: IP address allocation via APNIC (foreign RIR functions)
s-3-2-4.previewHtml: Shared dependency: When allocation through the regional chain is unreachable, You can stand up new address space fails with it. No alternative path in the fault trees of What your service sits on: four fault trees routes around the chain, and no other top event depends on this dependency.

s-3-2-5.title: Access networks and address translation
s-3-2-5.previewHtml: Shared dependency: When access networks fail, four top events fail with them: Your users load your service, Your users get notified, Your users message and call each other and Your users log in, each through an AND gate. Online checkout approves fails with them, and Your users pay survives only through its Card-present domestic authorization clears branch.

s-3-3.title: Application infrastructure
s-3-3.previewHtml: The application-infrastructure layer group differs from the network layer group in where failure starts. Network chokepoints cut or waste international capacity while the cables stay intact. Application-infrastructure dependencies sit above the network layer. They fail when the foreign-operated services that packets are addressed to become unreachable, even though packets still travel.

s-3-3-1.title: DNS resolution
s-3-3-1.previewHtml: Shared dependency: When name resolution fails, three top events fail with it: Your users load your service, Your cloud-hosted data is readable and writable, and Online checkout approves. Each fails through an AND gate, so no alternative path in the “What your service sits on: four fault trees” section's trees routes around it.

s-3-3-2.title: TLS/PKI & trust
s-3-3-2.previewHtml: Shared dependency: When the trust chain fails, seven top events fail with it: users cannot load the service (Your users load your service), cloud-hosted and domestically hosted data cannot be read or written (Your cloud-hosted data is readable and writable, Your domestically hosted data is readable and writable), users cannot log in (Your users log in), online checkout cannot approve (Your users pay), software cannot ship (You can ship and update software), and the team cannot detect and respond to an attack (You can detect and respond to an attack). Each is an AND position, so no alternative path in the “What your service sits on: four fault trees” section's trees routes around the dependency; card-present payment, the domestic branch of Your users pay, is the only part of Tree 3 it does not reach.

s-3-3-3.title: Time
s-3-3-3.previewHtml: Shared dependency: When the time hierarchy or its validity windows fail, Time holds fails with them, since the hierarchy is an AND child of Time holds, and with Time holds fall Your users load your service, Your users log in, and Online checkout approves. The authenticator-app alternative under Second-factor delivery rests on Time holds alone and falls too, leaving second-factor delivery to the messaging infrastructure of Messaging infrastructure.

s-3-3-4.title: Push fan-out
s-3-3-4.previewHtml: Shared dependency: When push fan-out fails, Your users get notified fails with it, and no alternative path in the “What your service sits on: four fault trees” section's trees routes around it. You can see your service and be paged survives only while messaging infrastructure (Messaging infrastructure), the other alternative under Page delivery, carries the page.

s-3-3-5.previewHtml: Shared dependency: When identity and access fails, three top events fail with it: Your cloud-hosted data is readable and writable, Your users log in, and You can control your infrastructure. Each is an AND position, so no alternative path in the “What your service sits on: four fault trees” section's trees routes around the dependency.

s-3-3-6.previewHtml: Shared dependency: When the software supply chain fails, You can ship and update software and You can detect and respond to an attack fail with it. s-3-3-7.previewHtml: Shared dependency: When the foreign edge-delivery path or a render-critical embed fails, Your users load your service fails with it. The gate is an AND whose scope in What your service sits on: four fault trees is render-critical assets, the trees draw no alternative path around it, and no other top event depends on this dependency.

Those are the only two children of the OR gate of Your users pay, so Your users pay itself fails, and no other top event depends on this dependency.

s-3-3-10.previewHtml: Shared dependency: When messaging infrastructure fails, Your users message and call each other fails with it: the gate is an AND with no alternative in the trees of What your service sits on: four fault trees. s-3-3-11.previewHtml: Shared dependency: When session control and NAT traversal relays fail, Your users message and call each other fails with them. No alternative path in the trees of What your service sits on: four fault trees routes around the dependency, and no other top event depends on it.

s-3-3-13.previewHtml: Shared dependency: When observability and paging fail, two top events fail with them: You can see your service and be paged and You can detect and respond to an attack. Both are AND gates, so no alternative path in the trees of What your service sits on: four fault trees routes around them.

s-3-3-14.previewHtml: Shared dependency: When security operations fail, one top event fails with them: You can detect and respond to an attack. It is an AND gate, so no alternative path in the trees of What your service sits on: four fault trees routes around it.

s-3-3-15.previewHtml: Shared dependency: When replicated state loses its quorum, one top event fails with it: Your domestically hosted data is readable and writable. It is an AND gate, so no alternative path in the trees of What your service sits on: four fault trees routes around it.

s-3-4.title: Human-organizational dependencies
s-3-4.previewHtml: The OSI model accounts for every byte that crosses the network, but it has no layer for people and organizations. It has no layer for the person who holds a server's root credentials. It has none for the organization that must still exist three years after launch to apply security patches. It has none for the community that moderates content when a crisis fills a platform with misinformation.

s-4-0.title: Reading key
s-4-0.previewHtml: Chapter 3 located the shared dependencies through which each disruption level reaches civilian services. This chapter lists the measures that engineers can build, configure, integrate, or adopt against each dependency before a disruption begins. This reading key explains how every section is labeled. Decision guide, after Interfaces, turns the measures into a decision guide: what each capability loses in each hosting posture, what to prepare first, six organization profiles, and a drill.

s-4-4.title: Shared substrate sections
s-4-4.previewHtml: Each of the four sections below covers one substrate (what must still be working for a measure to work) that several threads depend on; the threads cite the section by name and do not restate it.

s-4-4-1.title: Site LAN, sync-when-possible
s-4-4-1.previewHtml: Restores: (Structural inference from the local-first data, pre-provisioned identity, local registry, LAN messaging, and local name-resolution mechanisms cited in this section's solution blocks) Top events Your users message and call each other (messaging), Your domestically hosted data is readable and writable (local data write), Your users log in (authentication), and You can ship and update software (deployment) remain operable within the site while no upstream network path is available. A top event is the outcome at the top of a fault tree in What your service sits on: four fault trees. State that has diverged is reconciled when any path returns, whether LAN, satellite, or radio.

s-4-4-2.title: Satellite terminal operated by the solution
s-4-4-2.previewHtml: Restores: (Structural inference from the What your service sits on: four fault trees base-tree Offshore path holds dependency chain, the OneWeb gateways in Japan and Thailand reported by Digitimes, and Cloudflare's Ukraine traffic analysis) The terminal gives its host site an offshore IP path through Offshore path holds, one of the base trees (the fault trees of What your service sits on: four fault trees that several capabilities share). Every top event (the outcome at the top of a fault tree) that depends on Offshore path holds regains its path, up to the throughput ceiling of Satellite Trickle.

s-4-4-3.title: Off-grid radio
s-4-4-3.previewHtml: Restores: Top event Your users message and call each other, users exchanging text messages with each other, without any IP path. A top event is the outcome at the top of a fault tree in What your service sits on: four fault trees. (Structural inference from the Meshtastic, Reticulum, and Bitchat device-to-device radio designs cited in this section) Messages travel directly between devices by radio, at the rate that the shared channel allows, which is narrow by design. The designs need no Internet infrastructure, but a deployment has that property only if it is built that way. A Meshtastic node with an Internet connection can forward packets to and from an MQTT server, which joins the local mesh to users on the Internet (Meshtastic, MQTT Module Configuration, accessed November 2026). In a packet log that a participant kept at one node on Taipei's public mesh during the mobile-data slowdown of the 2026 Urban Resilience Exercise, on August 13, the share of received packets that had come through MQTT rose from 21% to 27%, and 7 of the 20 MQTT gateways in the log disappeared during the exercise (Public account by a participant who logged mesh traffic at one node in Taipei, August 2026).

s-4-4-4.title: No network
s-4-4-4.previewHtml: Restores: (Structural inference from the cached-content, offline-map, and pre-provisioned-credential mechanisms cited in this section) A function served entirely by pre-provisioned material can operate without a usable network path, including within an isolated segment during Island Partition: cached content pages and offline map tiles restore reach-and-communicate on each device that holds them; physically transported software artifacts and configuration restore operate-and-deploy across the partition line; bulk data on removable media restores store-and-retrieve for records prepared before the disruption; a float of cash and pre-loaded stored-value cards restores authenticate-and-transact at points of sale that would otherwise need a live authorization; and offline runbooks and pre-provisioned credentials extend operate-and-deploy and authenticate-and-transact to operations that would otherwise need a live control plane.

s-4-6.title: Decision guide
s-4-6.previewHtml: This section is for the developer or IT lead in Taiwan who has to decide where a service is hosted and what to prepare first. It draws on the fault trees of What your service sits on: four fault trees and the blocks of Physical-stratum threads to Shared substrate sections and does not repeat them. It has four parts. Capability-loss matrix shows what each capability loses at each level, for four hosting postures. Coverage ordering by effort tier orders the Chapter 4 blocks by how much they cover for how much effort. Six organization profiles applies both to six kinds of organization. The egress-blocked drill describes a drill that lets one organization fill in its own row of the matrix.

s-5-1.title: The shared trade-off
s-5-1.previewHtml: The measures in Chapter 4 share one structure: each measure keeps a service responding by giving something up in advance. In Chapter 4, the line labeled Property traded away names that cost for each measure. This section introduces the vocabulary of that line: the triad of confidentiality, integrity and availability (the CIA triad). The triad frames the trade-off lines of Chapter 4: the sentence on each line opens with one of the three terms, with Possession, or with Nothing. Possession, control over where a copy, key or device physically or legally sits, is the one cost outside the triad that the line names, and Research limitations sets out why the report adds it. The report defines and discusses the triad only in Chapter 5.

s-5-2.title: The DIE triad
s-5-2.previewHtml: The DIE triad is a counterpart to the CIA triad that describes how a system is designed. Sounil Yu proposed distributed, immutable and ephemeral as design principles for systems built as interchangeable "cattle" rather than individually tended "pets". Yu argued that these attributes "can actually counter the need for the CIA triad" (Yu, How to Prioritize Security Controls for Sensitive Data and Applications in AWS, AWS Marketplace, March 2020). Yu presented the model at the RSA Conference in 2020 (TechTarget, Experts say CIA security triad needs a DIE model upgrade, March 2020).

s-5-3.title: Research limitations
s-5-3.previewHtml: The report analyzes effects, not likelihood, and therefore gives no estimate of risk. Risk is a function of the likelihood of a threat event and of its adverse impact (NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1, Guide for Conducting Risk Assessments, September 2012). The report models only impact and how impact spreads. This choice follows capabilities-based planning, which plans under uncertainty for a wide range of challenges instead of against one specific threat and scenario (Davis, Analytic Architecture for Capabilities-Based Planning, Mission-System Analysis, and Transformation, RAND MR-1513, 2002). The choice has a cost. The decision guide of Decision guide orders the measures by tier of effort and, within a tier, by how many of the fault trees' top events each one helps restore, so a reader can see which preparation covers most for least work. The ordering still rests on no likelihood: it is not a risk ranking, and it cannot say which preparation will repay its cost first.

s-5-4.title: Further research
s-5-4.previewHtml: The 22 open items of the Known Gaps appendix are the first agenda for further research. The other five, F-3, F-9, F-10, F-11 and F-14, have been superseded by sections of Chapter 3. This chapter groups the 22 open items by the method that each item would need, and the appendix does not make this grouping. The items fall into four sets:

s-5-5.title: Concluding remarks
s-5-5.previewHtml: A server in Taiwan is the price of entry, not the answer (The short answer). What keeps a service working through a cutoff is preparation done while the cables are whole: in the lab, an ordinary service changed with Chapter 4 measures alone passed all 15 of its probes under both bounds of the cut, covering ten of its eleven functions; certificate renewal was not tested (Appendix A, §A.4).

s-a-0.title: Appendix A: Measurements and cutoff lab
s-a-0.previewHtml: Most of this report rests on documents: standards, operator posts, incident write-ups and measurement studies by others. This appendix holds the evidence the report gathered itself. In the early hours of 13 November 2026, Taiwan time, a set of scripts in this repository asked a few hundred Taiwanese services, and the infrastructure under them, a narrow question: when a packet leaves a home broadband line in Taiwan, where does the thing that answers it sit? The answers place endpoints on the island or off it. They do not show what keeps working once the cables are cut, and every finding below says which of the two it can support.

s-a-1.title: Method and limits
s-a-1.previewHtml: Vantage. Every measurement in Measurements was made from one fixed-broadband line in Taiwan on HiNet, autonomous system AS3462. F29 is not a measurement from this line or from this window: it is a field observation of September 2026, of the fourth kind defined below. The modules ran in three sessions inside one window, from 16:23 to 17:55 UTC on 12 November 2026; the data files carry a timestamp on every row. In Taiwan time that window fell on the night of 12 to 13 November, from 00:23 to 01:55 on 13 November, so a date of 13 November elsewhere in the report refers to the same measurements; this appendix gives every date in UTC. The line's address, its hostname and its first network hops are recorded nowhere in the published data, and this appendix does not give them. The vantage had no IPv6 route, so every measurement is IPv4.

s-a-2.title: Measurements
s-a-2.previewHtml: This part holds 29 findings. The 28 findings of the November study keep the numbers they were given when the study was run, F1 to F28, so that a citation such as (Appendix A, F7) always points at the same result. F29, at the end, was added on 14 November 2026 and stands apart: it is the author's unlogged account of a field test of September 2026, of the kind Method and limits calls field observation, unlogged, and nothing in the rest of this paragraph applies to it. Each finding gives what was measured, how many and when, the result, the kind of evidence as defined in Method and limits (necessary-only, conclusive or direct reading), and what it cannot show. Every finding except F18 and F19, which read public routing data, comes from the one vantage of Method and limits: a fixed-broadband line on HiNet (AS3462) in Taiwan, IPv4 only, measured in one window from 16:23 to 17:55 UTC on 12 November 2026, which was 00:23 to 01:55 on 13 November in Taiwan. Dates below are UTC. The on-island bound is 8.17 ms and the offshore bound 14.71 ms. Every number was recomputed from the data file named with the finding, all of them in docs/research/measurements-2026-11/.

s-a-3.title: Cutoff-lab census
s-a-3.previewHtml: Measurements shows where things answer. The census asks the next question: when the international links are gone, does the home page still render? On 13 November 2026 the lab loaded the home pages of the same 300 target domains (Method and limits) in a real browser under nine conditions: an ordinary visit, two settings of a modelled 50% Degradation, and six readings of Global Cutoff that differ in which on-island nodes survive and whether resolver caches still hold names. Each cut was applied on the lab's own side of the connection, and nothing outside the lab was impaired. The rows are in docs/research/cutoff-lab-2026-11/census/: results.jsonl for the warm runs, cold-results.jsonl for the cold-DNS runs and c1-results.jsonl for the Degradation model, with the harness in scripts/cutoff-lab/. Every number below was recomputed from those files.

s-a-4.title: Reference stack and verification table
s-a-4.previewHtml: Cutoff-lab census cuts the connection under other people's home pages. This part asks the report's own question of a service that an engineer builds: when the international links are gone, which of its functions keep working, and do the measures of Chapter 4 hold up when someone actually applies them? The lab wrote down an ordinary small service as one probe per function, ran it as a typical team ships it, then changed each function with one Chapter 4 measure and ran it again. The probes are in scripts/cutoff-lab/e2/, and the raw rows in docs/research/cutoff-lab-2026-11/e2/data/ (results-asshipped.jsonl, results-asshipped-run1.jsonl, results-hardened.jsonl). Every count below was recomputed from those rows.

s-a-5.title: Clock-cascade timeline
s-a-5.previewHtml: Cutoff-lab census and Reference stack and verification table show what fails in the first hours of a cut. This part follows what the calendar takes away afterwards: certificates, signatures, tokens and cached records that were valid when the cables went and expire one by one, with nobody able to renew them. Day 0 is 13 November 2026, the day after the measurements of Measurements. The question for each row is the same: if nothing is renewed, by which day has this stopped, and for whom?

known-gaps.title: Appendix: Known Gaps (F-Items from Pre-Composition Research)
known-gaps.previewHtml: Purpose. This appendix records 27 candidate items. Research before composition nominated each item as a possible shared dependency. Each item was then assessed against the report's definition of a single point of failure (SPOF), given in How to read a SPOF walk. Each item initially failed to meet the definition for at least one of three reasons. First, the dependency was not shared in the required sense: it was tooling that is consumed directly, with no services sitting on it. Second, the evidence could not support a full level-by-level trace without further field research. Third, the item fell outside the scope of the engineer audience that this report addresses.
